Any form of physical contact with others

vignette:
Malik was nineteen, an African American detective who still looked younger than his badge suggested, with a careful manner that had made him seem composed to colleagues and clients alike. That composure had been tested several months earlier, when he was held captive during an ordeal he still struggled to put into words. When he tried to speak about it, he often stalled in the middle of a sentence, aware of the facts yet unable to shape them into a clean account. He would say only that it had been “bad” or “a mess,” then fall silent, his jaw tightening as though language itself had become unreliable. What he did not say was often more vivid in his body than in speech: there were moments when, without any clear picture in his mind, the full emotional force of what had happened would crash back over him, leaving him tense, hot, and briefly disconnected from the room around him. At other times, a sound would rise in his head with such force that it seemed to drown out the present; he described hearing fragments of what he had heard during the frightening event, especially sharp voices and the rough edges of noises that had accompanied the captivity. These intrusions did not arrive as complete scenes he could narrate from beginning to end, but as impressions, sensations, and auditory echoes that made him go still.

In the months after he was released, Malik began trying hard not to think about the trauma. He found himself actively pushing away any line of thought that approached it, redirecting his attention the moment he sensed memories coming close. At first he tried to outrun them through work, telling himself that staying busy would keep his mind from circling back, but he noticed that the effort of suppressing the memories was exhausting in itself. He started monitoring his own thoughts, bracing whenever a silence stretched too long or whenever he became aware that his mind had drifted toward the event. The more he fought to keep it out of awareness, the more he noticed how quickly his body could react when something reminded him of it, especially at night. Darkness had become a particular problem. Malik avoided going out after dark and would arrange his evenings so that he was inside before night fell whenever possible. If he had to be outdoors after sunset, he stayed close to lit areas and moved with visible tension, scanning the environment in a way that was difficult for him to explain to others. What frightened him most was the sense that night made him vulnerable in the same way he had once been vulnerable, when he could not easily tell what was happening around him. The ordinary quiet of evening, rather than feeling restful, made him feel exposed.

His avoidance extended to touch as well. Malik began pulling back from any physical contact with others, even the casual gestures that had once seemed unremarkable. He stiffened when someone reached for his shoulder, recoiled from quick greetings, and made excuses to avoid hugs. This had become a strain in his relationship, because the person he was dating did not understand why he now seemed to flinch from even gentle contact. Malik felt ashamed of the change but could not bring himself to force it. In intimate moments, he became acutely aware of where someone else’s hand might land on his body, and that awareness alone could make him tense. He did not describe this as fear of a specific person so much as a refusal to let anyone close enough for his body to register touch without warning.

At work, these changes were increasingly difficult to hide. Detective work demanded long hours, unpredictable schedules, and frequent movement through the city at times when Malik now preferred to be indoors. He noticed that evening assignments left him on edge, especially when he had to step outside after dark or wait in dimly lit areas. He managed to keep functioning, but he did so by organizing his life around the need to keep certain experiences away from him. Over time, that left him more isolated, more tired, and less willing to accept social plans that might stretch into the night. Friends commented that he seemed distant; his partner noticed how carefully he avoided touch. Malik himself experienced the changes less as a theory than as a daily discipline of holding himself together, never quite letting his thoughts settle where they wanted to go.

He finally sought help after realizing how much space the trauma had taken up in his life. The PCL-5 score of 63 fit with the way he described feeling overwhelmed by reminders he could not fully explain. What brought him in was not a single dramatic breakdown, but the accumulation of nights avoided, conversations cut short, and the growing sense that he was living around the edges of his own experience. He said he wanted to be able to talk about what happened without losing his words and to move through the night without bracing for it. More than anything, Malik hoped to stop feeling as though his body and mind were still trapped somewhere back in the event, and he feared that if nothing changed, the distance he had built from other people would keep widening.
